title: When Assessment Becomes a Conversation
author: Episcopal Academy Center for Teaching and Learning
summary: Episcopal Academy pilots Viva, an oral assessment platform that shifts evaluation from written products to students' real-time ability to explain and reason aloud. The tool scales oral assessment by pairing student writing with AI-generated follow-up questions, making the conversation visible and forcing students to own their thinking in real time rather than relying on distance and revision. Rather than safeguarding against AI-generated work, Viva functions as a process speed bump where explanation becomes unavoidable, though implementation raises real questions about anxiety, language processing, and how accommodations translate into spoken formats.
points: Oral assessment at scale changes how students show up: the camera triggers alertness and ownership, forcing explanation over revision.
Viva shifts evaluation from measuring written products to assessing students' real-time ability to explain, connect, and reason aloud.
Structured questioning transforms a scaling problem into a feasible tool for teachers, making oral signal gatherable at a cadence that informs instruction.
The format functions as a process speed bump: because students must explain ideas in real time and respond to AI-generated questions, generation without understanding becomes hard to hide.
Implementation is intentionally formative; real questions remain about anxiety, language processing, and how accommodations work in oral formats.
quotes: What we’re really interested in exploring is how Viva enables a more direct, spoken form of assessment—at scale. This isn’t about replacing written work, but about revealing layers of understanding that written artifacts alone often fail to show.

There’s a noticeable shift in posture and attention: students become more alert, more present, and more engaged with their own thinking. The format can feel slightly intimidating at first—yet that discomfort is part of what makes it valuable.” “It asks students to take ownership of their ideas in real time, rather than relying on distance, polish, or revision. And in the AI era, this sort of just-in-time conversational competency has real value.
Oral assessments surface whether students can explain, connect, and reason with ideas—not just reproduce them. They make understanding visible in ways written work often cannot.

What interests us about Viva is that it meaningfully changes this constraint. By structuring and scaling the questioning process, it makes oral assessment possible in contexts where it has traditionally been out of reach—not as a replacement for teacher judgment, but as a way to make those judgments more informed and more feasible.

Viva doesn’t function primarily as a safeguard; it functions more as a speed bump to generating one’s work with AI assistance. Because students must explain ideas aloud, in real time, and in response to questions generated directly from their own writing, the assessment shifts from product to process.
Oral assessment introduces real questions about access and fairness: how it intersects with anxiety, language processing, neurodiversity, and the accommodations many students understandably rely on.

We’re not treating Viva as a finished solution. We’re treating it as a design space: a chance to figure out how oral explanation can become a fair, repeatable part of how students demonstrate understanding.” Archived from Episcopal Academy CTL (Substack) on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
